hook: You can get a barista‑style espresso from a vending machine in under a minute in Korea.
body: Every 24‑hour convenience store in Seoul houses a sleek coffee machine that grinds beans, froths milk, and serves a latte in about 30 seconds. The machines use RFID cards or mobile payments, and the drinks are personalized via a touchscreen menu. This convenience has helped Korea become one of the world’s biggest per‑capita coffee consumers, with vending coffee sales surpassing 1 billion cups a year.

label: Air‑Aware Streetlights
topic: Seoul’s streetlights change color to signal real‑time air quality
hook: The streetlights in Seoul change color with the air!
body: Since a pilot began in 2020 and expanded in 2022, Seoul has been installing smart LED poles that typically glow blue when PM2.5 levels are low and shift to amber or red when pollution rises. The lights also dim during low‑traffic hours, which is estimated to reduce municipal electricity use by about 20 %.
twist: The same network feeds data to a public app, letting residents see neighborhood‑by‑neighborhood air maps in real time.

topic: Korean companies use apps to order identical lunches for the whole office

label: The ‘‑ssi’ Slip
topic: Korean honorific ‘‑ssi’ is used like ‘Mr./Ms.’ but can sound overly formal in casual texts
hook: 한국 친구에게 문자를 보냈는데 ‘‑씨?’라는 반응을 받은 적 있나요? – 흔한 한국어 예절 포인트입니다.
body: 한국어에서 ‘‑씨’는 이름 뒤에 붙는 정중한 호칭으로, 영어의 Mr.나 Ms.와 비슷하지만 관계와 상황에 따라 뉘앙스가 다릅니다. 보통은 이름 또는 성+이름 뒤에 붙이며, 비슷한 지위의 동료나 지인에게 자연스럽습니다. 다만 성만 붙인 ‘김 씨’는 무례하거나 거리감 있게 들릴 수 있어 피하는 것이 좋습니다.
twist: 친한 친구나 비격식 채팅에서는 ‘‑씨’를 생략하기도 하지만, 윗사람에게는 ‘‑씨’보다 직함+‘님’을 쓰는 편이 안전합니다.

narration: Ever text a Korean friend and get a confused “‑ssi?” – it’s a common Korean etiquette point. In Korean, ‑ssi is a polite suffix attached to a person’s given name or full name, similar to “Mr.” or “Ms.” It is most natural with colleagues, acquaintances, or people of a similar social position. But avoid attaching it to only a surname: “Kim‑ssi” can sound distant or rude. In casual chats with close friends, people often drop it for a softer tone. The twist: with a boss, teacher, or much older person, a title plus “‑nim” is usually safer than “‑ssi.” So use “Jimin‑ssi” with a peer, but “Manager Kim‑nim” with your manager.
fact_issues: Overgeneralized claim that dropping ‘‑ssi’ in professional emails is always seen as disrespectful – changed to ‘often’ and noted it can vary.
Implied that all Koreans drop ‘‑ssi’ in digital chats – softened to ‘many people’.
narration_original: Ever text a Korean friend and get a confused “‑ssi?” – it’s a common etiquette trap. In Korean, ‑ssi is a polite suffix like “Mr.” or “Ms.” attached to a name. In face‑to‑face conversation, especially with strangers or seniors, you’ll hear ‑ssi used regularly. But in digital chats most people drop it for brevity. That’s why a foreigner might write “Jimin‑ssi, 오늘 회의 어때?” and get a puzzled reply of just “씨?” Using ‑ssi in informal messages can feel stiff and create distance, while leaving it off when texting a senior may seem disrespectful. The twist: in professional emails, adding ‑ssi after a full name signals seniority, whereas omitting it can be read as a lack of respect. So next time, think twice before you type that suffix.

topic: Korean food delivery, especially from Korean restaurants, often includes complimentary side dishes alongside the main order.

body: When customers order Korean food through delivery apps such as Baedal Minjok or Coupang Eats, participating restaurants often include banchan—such as kimchi, pickled radish, or seasoned vegetables—with the main dish. hook: Did you know many people in Seoul use cafés as quiet places to study and work?

However, rules differ by café, and some chains have introduced guidance for customers who occupy seats for very long periods or bring large equipment.

label: Respectful Drink Pour
topic: Koreans pour drinks for elders with both hands as a sign of respect
hook: Ever seen a Korean pour a drink with two hands and wonder why?
body: In Korean drinking etiquette, pouring for someone older or more senior is a way to show respect. A person commonly holds the bottle with the right hand while supporting the right forearm or wrist with the left hand. The person receiving the drink may also hold the glass with both hands or support it with the other hand. This custom is especially associated with soju and other shared drinks, though the level of formality depends on age, relationship, and setting. Among close friends of similar age, a more casual one-handed pour may be acceptable.
twist: It is also considered polite to receive a drink from an elder with both hands, often with a slight bow.
caveat: The two‑handed pour is common in many formal meals, especially with older family members, but younger friends may pour more casually.

label: 1000‑Day Celebration
topic: Baek‑il, a Korean milestone birthday celebrated 1,000 days after birth
hook: Did you know Korean families often celebrate a baby’s 100th day?
body: In South Korea, many families celebrate a baby’s 100th day, called “baek-il.” The celebration often includes a simple family gathering and foods such as baekseolgi, a plain white steamed rice cake, and seaweed soup. Traditionally, baekseolgi was shared with others in the hope that blessings and good health would return to the baby. The day is a meaningful family milestone, though how families celebrate it varies widely today. Some keep the ceremony simple at home, while others take commemorative photos or hold a small gathering.
twist: Baek-il is different from doljanchi, the larger first-birthday celebration held when a baby turns one year old.
caveat: Baek‑il is celebrated by many families, especially in more traditional households, but not universally practiced across all regions or among all age groups.

서울 곳곳에 자동 판매기가 거의 매 블록마다 설치돼 있어 음료는 물론 신선한 과일, 즉석 라면, 마스크, 심지어 방수 우산까지 판매합니다. 기계는 온도 조절이 가능하고 신용카드·모바일 결제도 받아 여름엔 차가운 사과, 겨울엔 따뜻한 차를 가게에 들어가지 않고도 구매할 수 있습니다. 이 촘촘한 네트워크는 빠른 생활 리듬과 즉석 편의에 대한 높은 수요에서 탄생했습니다. 많은 역에는 계절에 따라 재고를 바꾸는 ‘멀티‑상품’ 자동 판매기도 있습니다.

label: Toilet Sound Masking
topic: Public restrooms play music to hide bathroom noises
hook: Did you know many Korean restrooms play a song when you flush?
body: In many subway stations, malls, and office buildings across South Korea, the toilets are equipped with speakers that emit a short melody or ambient sound each time the flush button is pressed. The practice started as a privacy measure to mask the sounds of flushing, which can be considered embarrassing in public. The music is usually a simple pop tune or a gentle chime, and it stops after a few seconds. Visitors often comment that it feels like the bathroom is singing.
twist: Some locations even synchronize the music with the building’s public announcement system, so the same song plays across all restrooms on a floor.
caveat: The music is common in newer public facilities in major cities, but many older or rural restrooms still use silent flushes.
verify_note: Korean restroom music, toilet sound masking, public bathroom flush music South Korea

The music is simple, often a catchy jingle, and many visitors say the bathroom feels like it’s singing. 한국 전역의 지하철역, 쇼핑몰, 사무실 건물 등에서 화장실에 스피커가 설치돼 물 내리는 버튼을 누를 때마다 짧은 멜로디나 배경음이 재생됩니다. 이 관행은 물 내리는 소리를 가리기 위한 프라이버시 조치로 시작됐으며, 공공장소에서 부끄러워할 수 있는 소리를 가릴 수 있습니다. 음악은 보통 간단한 팝 튠이나 부드러운 차임이며 몇 초 후에 멈춥니다. 방문객들은 화장실이 노래를 부르는 듯하다고 종종 말합니다.

💡 일부 장소에서는 건물의 안내 방송 시스템과 음악을 동기화해 같은 층에 있는 모든 화장실에서 같은 곡이 동시에 재생되기도 합니다.

label: QR‑Only Street Food
topic: Many street vendors now accept only mobile QR payments
hook: Ever tried buying tteokbokki with just a QR code?
body: Since 2020, a growing number of street food stalls in Seoul’s night markets have replaced cash registers with QR‑code payment stickers from apps like KakaoPay and Toss. Customers scan the code on the vendor’s cart, enter the amount, and the payment is confirmed instantly, eliminating the need for change. Vendors say the system speeds up service and reduces the risk of theft, while customers appreciate the convenience of not carrying cash late at night. The trend is most visible around areas like Myeongdong and Hongdae.
twist: Some vendors offer a small discount of about 5 % for QR payments, encouraging the shift away from cash.
caveat: The QR‑only model is common in busy urban night markets but many traditional stalls, especially in smaller towns, still rely primarily on cash.

ko_description:
🎯 단지 QR 코드만으로 떡볶이를 구매해본 적이 있나요?

2020년부터 서울 야시장에 있는 길거리 음식 가판대가 현금 계산대 대신 카카오페이, 토스 같은 앱의 QR‑코드 결제 스티커로 교체되고 있습니다. 고객은 가판대에 부착된 코드를 스캔하고 금액을 입력하면 결제가 즉시 확인되어 거스름돈이 필요 없습니다. 가판대 주인들은 이 시스템이 서비스 속도를 높이고 절도 위험을 줄여준다고 말하며, 늦은 밤 현금을 들고 다니지 않아도 되는 편리함을 고객이 좋아합니다. 이 트렌드는 명동, 홍대 같은 지역에서 가장 두드러집니다.

label: Han River Grill Kiosks
topic: You can rent a portable charcoal grill at the Han River parks via a kiosk
hook: Did you know you can rent a mini grill for a picnic right by the river with just a tap?
body: Along the Han River’s popular parks, automated kiosks allow visitors to rent small charcoal grills, a set of tongs, and a fire‑starter for a nominal fee. After scanning a QR code and paying through a mobile app, the grill is unlocked and can be used at any designated picnic spot for up to two hours. The service was introduced to encourage outdoor cooking while keeping the park clean, as the grills are collected and cleaned by park staff after use. Families and friends often gather to grill samgyeopsal or vegetables while enjoying the night skyline.
twist: If the grill is returned before the time limit, the app refunds the remaining minutes as a discount for the next rental.
caveat: The grill‑rental kiosks are available at major river parks in Seoul, such as Yeouido and Banpo, but smaller riverside areas may not offer the service.

label: Umbrella Vending Machines
topic: Disposable umbrellas sold from vending machines at subway stations
hook: Caught in a sudden Seoul downpour? You can grab an umbrella from a vending machine.
body: In many subway stations and busy streets, small transparent vending machines dispense single‑use plastic umbrellas for a few thousand won. The machines are stocked year‑round, and the umbrellas fold automatically when you push the button. This convenience grew after the city saw a rise in spontaneous rainstorms and commuters needing quick protection without carrying one. Many locals treat it as a backup, keeping a few in lockers or bags.
twist: Some machines also offer a tiny bottle of hand sanitizer alongside the umbrella.
caveat: The service is common in major cities like Seoul and Busan, but not universal across all neighborhoods or smaller towns.

label: Emoji‑Only Messaging
topic: Korean teens often converse using only emojis and short phrases on KakaoTalk
hook: Ever seen a whole conversation made up of just emojis? Korean teens do it daily.
body: On KakaoTalk, South Korea’s dominant messaging app, many younger users have developed a style of chatting that relies heavily on emojis, stickers, and abbreviated slang, sometimes sending entire sentences without a single alphabetic character. This visual language speeds up replies and adds emotional nuance, especially in fast‑paced group chats. The trend reflects Korea’s high smartphone penetration and the app’s rich sticker marketplace, which offers culturally specific icons. It’s common to see a series of heart, fire, and laughing emojis replace a detailed explanation.

label: Café Passport Hopping
topic: Friends race to collect stamps at themed cafés across Seoul
hook: Did you know many Seoul cafés hand out stamp cards so you can turn a coffee run into a treasure hunt?
body: In many neighborhoods, cafés offer a small card that gets a stamp for each visit, often with a cute illustration tied to the shop's theme. label: Mobile Library Bus
topic: A book‑laden bus stops at subway stations, letting commuters borrow on the spot
hook: Imagine waiting for your train and picking up a novel from a moving library truck.
body: Seoul’s municipal library runs a specially designed bus that travels along major subway lines during rush hour, stocked with a rotating selection of best‑sellers and children’s books. caveat: The mobile library operates on weekdays during peak commuting hours and focuses on central districts; coverage may be limited in outlying suburbs.

topic: High‑speed trains equipped with personal power outlets and free Wi‑Fi for on‑the‑go work

label: Bike‑Tree Parking Robot
topic: Automated bike‑stacking robot lets cyclists park in a compact tower
hook: In Seoul, you can drop your bike into a robot that stacks it like a tree.
body: In the Seongsu‑Pangyo area, a machine called the Bike‑Tree (or Smart Bike Parking) automatically lifts, rotates, and stores bicycles vertically, creating a tower of bikes in a footprint of about two meters. The system uses sensors to identify the bike’s size and places it in an empty slot, then returns it when the owner scans a QR code. It was installed to solve limited sidewalk space and has become a popular sight for commuters and tourists alike. The service is managed by the local district and can be used via a mobile app or a membership card.
twist: The robot can hold up to 100 bikes while occupying less than 2 m² of ground space.
caveat: It is currently limited to a few pilot locations such as Seongsu, Pangyo, and some university campuses, not city‑wide.

label: Heated Public Toilets
topic: Many subway station restrooms feature heated toilet seats for winter comfort
hook: Ever sat on a warm toilet seat in a subway bathroom?
body: In major subway stations across Seoul and Busan, public restrooms are equipped with electric heated toilet seats that turn on automatically when the room temperature drops below a set point. The seats are powered by the station’s electricity and are especially common in newer stations built after 2010. This small comfort measure is intended to make winter commutes more pleasant for passengers who often need to use the facilities during rush hour. The heating is controlled centrally, so the seat stays warm even after the user leaves.
twist: Some models include a temperature sensor that adjusts the heat level based on the outside temperature, keeping the seat just above room temperature on the coldest days.
caveat: Heated seats are mainly found in newer or renovated stations and not in every public restroom, especially older ones in smaller cities.

label: Pepero Day Exchange
topic: November 11 is celebrated by swapping thin chocolate sticks as a friendly gesture
hook: On November 11, Koreans swap thin chocolate sticks like love letters.
body: Pepero Day, observed on 11/11 because the date resembles four stick-shaped snacks, has become a popular occasion for friends, classmates, and coworkers to give each other Pepero, a chocolate‑coated biscuit stick. The tradition started in the 1990s as a marketing event by a confectionery company and spread through schools and offices, where people often write short messages on the sticks. In recent years, many brands have released alternative flavors such as pretzel or almond, and some people use the day to give non‑chocolate gifts as a playful twist. While the day is widely recognized among younger generations, it is not an official holiday and many adults may simply ignore it.
twist: Some retailers report that Pepero sales on 11/11 can exceed the combined sales of the entire month of October.
caveat: The practice is most common among students and office workers in urban areas; it is not a nationwide public holiday.

label: ‘뭐해?’ Greeting
topic: 'What are you doing?' is often used as an informal way to say hello
hook: When a Korean says ‘What are you doing?’, they might just be saying hello.
body: In casual Korean conversation, especially among friends and younger people, the phrase ‘뭐해?’ (mwohae?) is frequently used as a greeting rather than a literal inquiry, similar to asking “What’s up?” in English. The speaker typically expects a brief response like “nothing” or “just working,” and the exchange serves to acknowledge the other person’s presence. This usage stems from a cultural tendency to start conversations with a light, open‑ended question that can be answered quickly. Because it is informal, it is usually avoided in formal settings or with elders, where a more polite greeting would be chosen.
twist: The same phrase can be heard on public transportation in Seoul, where commuters shout “뭐해?” to start a brief chat before boarding the train.
caveat: It is primarily used among peers and younger adults; older generations or formal contexts favor more respectful greetings.

topic: QR codes on small cards let Koreans share contact info instantly in cafés and meetings.

label: Underground Delivery Rooms
topic: Apartment complexes use secure underground rooms where couriers leave parcels for residents to pick up via an app.
hook: Ever wonder where 300 parcels a day disappear in a Seoul high‑rise? They’re waiting in a hidden underground room.
body: Many high‑rise apartment buildings in Seoul have a dedicated underground delivery room equipped with electronic lockers. Couriers place the package inside, the system records the recipient, and a push notification is sent to the resident’s smartphone. The resident opens the specific locker using a one‑time code or fingerprint, collects the item, and the locker relocks automatically. This setup reduces missed deliveries and keeps hallways clutter‑free.
twist: A growing number of complexes integrate facial recognition, allowing residents to open their locker simply by looking at a camera.
caveat: These delivery rooms are typical in newer or upscale complexes in Seoul and some other major cities; older buildings may still rely on door‑to‑door delivery.

label: Winter Shaved Ice
topic: Street vendors serve bingsu, a shaved‑ice dessert, even during Seoul’s freezing winter months.
hook: Yes, you can eat snow‑like ice cream in Seoul’s December chill—called bingsu.
body: In popular tourist spots like Myeongdong and Hongdae, street stalls set up insulated carts that serve bingsu year‑round. The shaved ice is topped with warm red bean paste, toasted rice cakes, and hot syrups, creating a contrast between the cold base and the comforting heat. Vendors often serve it in small disposable bowls, making it easy to enjoy while strolling through the night market. The practice started as a summer treat but persisted because the hot toppings keep customers warm.
twist: Some stalls even add a splash of hot chocolate or ginger tea over the ice, turning the dessert into an instant hand‑warmer.
caveat: Winter bingsu is most common in busy commercial districts and tourist areas; quieter neighborhoods may not have vendors offering it in cold weather.

label: Delivery Robots on Streets
topic: Autonomous robots bring food and parcels to doorsteps in Seoul neighborhoods
hook: Did you know tiny robots are already delivering pizza to Korean apartments?
body: In districts like Gangnam and Seongnam, companies operate small, box‑shaped delivery robots that travel on sidewalks. Residents receive a notification on their phone, open a door, and the robot slides a sealed bag onto a mat. The service is popular because it avoids traffic and contact during busy hours. It works mainly in upscale residential complexes that have a dedicated robot charging station.
twist: Some robots can climb a few steps, so they can reach the front door of a high‑rise building without an elevator.
caveat: The service is limited to certain neighborhoods and apartment complexes that have signed up for the pilot program; it is not yet city‑wide.

label: Smart Toilets with Music
topic: High‑tech public restrooms play a short tune after flushing to mask sounds
hook: Ever heard a bathroom sing after you finish?
body: Many public restrooms in Seoul’s subway stations and large malls are equipped with smart toilets that have heated seats, bidet functions, and a sound‑masking system. When a user flushes, a brief, soothing melody automatically plays for a few seconds. The feature was added to reduce embarrassment in crowded facilities and is controlled by motion sensors, so no extra button is needed.
twist: The same system can be set to play a different tune depending on the time of day, like a calm chime in the morning and a brighter jingle at night.
caveat: These smart toilets are common in newer or renovated public spaces, but older facilities may still have standard fixtures.

label: Black Day Jajangmyeon
topic: Singles gather on April 14th to eat black‑bean noodles as a playful holiday
hook: Why do some Koreans eat black noodles on a day called Black Day?
body: Two weeks after Valentine’s Day and White Day, South Korea observes Black Day on April 14th. Uncoupled friends and coworkers wear black clothing and meet at restaurants to share jajangmyeon, a noodle dish topped with dark soy‑bean sauce. The tradition started as a tongue‑in‑cheek response to the couple‑focused holidays, and many eateries offer special “Black Day” menus and discounts for groups in black attire.
twist: Some cafés even serve a dessert called “black coffee mousse” to keep the color theme consistent throughout the meal.
caveat: The celebration is most popular among younger adults in urban areas; not all Koreans observe Black Day.

label: QR‑Only Street Food
topic: Street vendors in Seoul accept only mobile QR payments, eliminating cash handling
hook: You can buy tteokbokki from a stall without ever pulling out a wallet.
body: In bustling food streets such as Hongdae and Gwangjang Market, many vendors now display a small QR code on a stand beside their stall. Customers scan the code with KakaoPay or other Korean mobile payment apps, select the menu on their phone, and pay instantly. A tiny thermal printer then issues a receipt with a number, and the vendor hands over the order when the number is called. This contact‑free system speeds up service and reduces the need for change.
twist: Some vendors also embed a short video of the dish’s preparation into the QR code, so diners can watch a quick clip while they wait.
caveat: The QR‑only system is common in popular tourist and nightlife districts, but many smaller or older stalls still accept cash.

A tiny thermal printer spits out a receipt with a number, and the vendor calls that number when your dish is ready. The contact‑free system speeds up service and cuts out the need for change. Some stalls even embed a short video of the cooking process in the QR code, so you can watch the sizzle while you wait. The QR‑only setup is common in popular tourist and nightlife areas, but many smaller or older stalls still take cash. Next time you crave street food, remember your phone might be the only thing you need.

country: Why Is Rice Cake So Important in Korea?
topic: Why do Koreans celebrate life with rice cakes?
hook: Why do Koreans celebrate life with rice cakes?
body: In Korea, rice cakes are more than just a sweet treat. They can mark some of life’s most important moments. For a baby’s first 100 days, families traditionally serve white rice cake called baekseolgi, symbolizing purity and wishes for a healthy life. Red bean rice cakes, known as pat-sirutteok, have traditionally been associated with warding off bad luck and wishing for good fortune. During Chuseok, Korea’s harvest holiday, families make songpyeon—small, half-moon-shaped rice cakes filled with ingredients like sesame seeds. Rice cakes are also shared with neighbors, given as gifts, and served at celebrations. Offering them can be a way to share happiness and good wishes. From welcoming a new baby to celebrating the harvest, Korean rice cakes carry wishes for health, happiness, and good fortune.
twist: Which one would you try first?

The warm broth contrasts with the cold air, and the tradition is seen as a way to welcome winter’s arrival. Children add a playful twist by making snow angels while waiting for the soup to cool. The practice has been highlighted in local news as a seasonal community activity.

Teachers track the waste amount, and the class with the lowest leftover volume receives a small reward, such as a potted plant for the classroom. The rest of the diners hold off on their own bowls until the elder finishes that first bite, then everyone begins together. This practice stems from Confucian values that prioritize seniority and communal harmony. Many restaurants in traditional districts still observe the custom for special meals.

hook: Imagine stepping off the train, taking a quick shower, then catching your next train—all without leaving the station.
body: Stations such as Seoul’s ‘Sangsu’ and ‘Hongik University’ have small shower stalls that can be used for a modest fee or free with a transit card balance. These facilities were added to encourage active commuting, allowing cyclists or early‑morning joggers to freshen up before heading into the office. The showers are gender‑separated, equipped with lockers and a towel‑service, and are cleaned multiple times a day. Signage in both Korean and English guides users on the usage procedure.
twist: Some stations integrate a drying cabinet that can warm a folded jacket while you shower.
caveat: Shower rooms are available only in a limited number of stations near major bike routes; most subway stations do not have this amenity.
verify_note: Seoul subway station public shower stalls Sangsu Hongik University bike commuters

label: Escalator Left‑Stand Rule
topic: In Seoul subway stations, people stand on the left side of escalators and walk up on the right.
hook: Did you know Seoul’s escalators have a hidden traffic rule?
body: When you step onto a subway escalator in Seoul, most commuters instinctively stand on the left side, leaving the right side clear for those who want to walk up or down. This habit stems from a city‑wide campaign launched in the 1990s to speed up rush‑hour flow. It’s reinforced by subtle floor markings and occasional signage, so even tourists quickly pick it up. The practice is most visible in busy hubs like Gangnam and Hongdae.
twist: In some stations, the left‑hand side is even equipped with a thin line of LED lights that flash when the escalator is crowded, nudging people to keep the right side free.
caveat: The left‑stand rule is common in major subway lines and many malls, but not all escalators in Korea follow it, especially in older buildings.
verify_note: Seoul escalator etiquette left side stand right side walk study 1990s campaign

label: Goat Café Latte
topic: Animal cafés in Seoul let you enjoy coffee while petting goats.
hook: Imagine sipping a latte while a goat nudges your hand—welcome to Seoul’s goat cafés!
body: In neighborhoods like Hongdae and Itaewon, several cafés blend a coffee shop with a small herd of goats that roam the indoor patio. Customers can order a drink and, after a brief safety briefing, feed or pet the goats that lounge among the tables. The concept grew from South Korea’s broader animal‑café trend, offering a therapeutic break for city dwellers. Staff often provide goat‑friendly snacks and encourage photo‑ops, making it a popular spot on Instagram.
twist: Some goat cafés even let patrons write their names on the goats’ ear tags for a small fee, turning the animal into a personalized souvenir.
caveat: Goat cafés are mainly found in trendy districts of Seoul and a few other cities; they are not present in every neighborhood.
verify_note: Seoul goat café Hongdae animal cafe goat latte Instagram trend

label: Friday Chicken Office
topic: Many Korean offices end the week with a group chicken‑and‑beer order placed through a shared app.
hook: Every Friday at 5 pm, Korean offices turn into a chicken‑and‑beer party—ordered with a single tap.
body: In numerous companies across Seoul, a rotating “order master” uses a mobile app like Baedal Minjok to order a bulk delivery of fried chicken and beer for the whole team. The food arrives just as the workday ends, and coworkers gather around a conference room to share the meal while chatting about the week. The cost is split automatically through the app’s payment feature, so no one has to handle cash. This ritual reinforces team bonding and is especially popular in tech startups and larger corporations alike.
twist: Some offices pair the chicken night with a quick round of “rock‑paper‑scissors” to decide who brings the next week’s dessert, turning the tradition into a playful competition.
caveat: While many firms in Seoul and other major cities adopt this practice, it is less common in smaller towns or more traditional industries.
verify_note: Korean office chicken beer Friday Baedal Minjok order tradition team bonding

label: Convenience Store Hot Counter
topic: Many Korean convenience stores cook fresh meals on‑site, not just heat pre‑made food.
hook: Did you know you can watch a chef flip tteokbokki inside a 24‑hour convenience store?
body: In major cities, chains like GS25 and CU have tiny kitchen counters where staff stir‑fry rice cakes, steam dumplings, and grill fish cakes right after you order. The food is prepared in minutes, so you get a steaming bowl that’s as fresh as a restaurant’s. This service runs all day and night, catering to commuters who need a hot bite after a late‑night subway ride.
twist: Some locations even let you customize the spice level by tapping a button on the ordering screen.
caveat: Not all convenience stores have a hot counter; the feature is common in urban outlets but rare in rural branches.
verify_note: GS25 hot food counter, CU convenience store fresh food, Korean convenience store tteokbokki made on site

label: Apartment Smart Lockers
topic: Apartment complexes use app‑controlled lockers for food delivery and parcel pick‑up.
hook: Imagine getting your lunch delivered to a locker in your building, not to your door.
body: Many newer apartment towers install networked lockers in the lobby that couriers place orders into. Residents receive a push notification with a one‑time code, walk to the locker, and retrieve a sealed container of bibimbap or a parcel. The system reduces missed deliveries and lets people collect items at any hour without waiting for a concierge.
twist: Some lockers have built‑in warming plates, so a hot meal stays warm until you open it.
caveat: These lockers are typical in large complexes in Seoul and Busan; older buildings or suburban apartments may not have them.
verify_note: Korea apartment smart lockers delivery, Korean apartment complex parcel locker, Korean building locker warm plate

label: KTX Quiet Car
topic: A whole carriage on high‑speed trains reserved for silence and focused work
hook: Did you know Korea’s bullet trains have a ‘silent car’ where you can actually work in peace?
body: On many KTX routes, one carriage is marked as a quiet zone. Passengers are asked to keep voices low, turn off phone ringtones, and use headphones. Business travelers often set up a mini‑office with a laptop, while families with infants are gently reminded to speak softly. The car is popular enough that commuters sometimes reserve seats in advance via the rail app.
twist: Some quiet‑car seats are equipped with a small power outlet and a personal lamp that automatically dims after 30 minutes to encourage short naps.
caveat: The quiet‑car policy applies mainly to major KTX lines and may not be enforced on all regional trains.
verify_note: KTX quiet car policy, Korean high-speed train silent car, KTX etiquette

label: Late‑Night Subway Food Court
topic: Underground eateries in Seoul stations stay open till the early morning for night‑shift crowds
hook: Ever wondered where a tired nurse can grab hot kimchi stew at 2 am in Seoul?
body: Several busy stations such as Hongdae, Gangnam, and Seoul Station host underground food courts that operate until 2–3 am. Vendors serve steaming bowls of noodle soup, tteokbokki, and ready‑made dosirak that arrive fresh from nearby kitchens. The lights stay on and the scent of broth fills the concourse, turning the subway into a late‑night dining hub. Many commuters treat it as a regular stop after their night shift or late study session.
twist: Some stalls use a ‘hot‑plate timer’ that automatically turns off the burner after 30 minutes to save energy and prevent fire hazards.
caveat: These extended‑hours food courts are found in major downtown stations; smaller suburban stations usually close by midnight.
verify_note: Seoul subway 24 hour food court, Hongdae station night food, late night subway eateries Korea

label: Daeboreum Sunrise Picnic
topic: Koreans greet the first full moon of the lunar year with a hilltop rice feast and ancient rituals
hook: Did you know Koreans climb hills at dawn on the first full moon to eat five‑grain rice for good luck?
body: On the 15th day of the lunar month, many Koreans head to a nearby hill or park before sunrise. They spread a blanket, share ogokbap – a mixed rice of five grains – and crack nuts together, a ritual called bureong that is believed to chase away bad spirits. The gathering mixes family bonding, a simple outdoor meal, and the hope that the first sunrise of the year will bring health and prosperity. While the practice is most visible in rural villages, city dwellers also join in at popular parks, turning the early morning into a communal celebration.
twist: In some regions participants also toss small rice cakes into the air, believing the floating grains will carry their wishes to the heavens.
caveat: The tradition is most common in certain neighborhoods and rural areas; many Koreans may not observe it, and the specific foods or rituals can vary by region.
verify_note: Daeboreum customs, ogokbap tradition, Korean first full moon sunrise, Jeongwol Daeboreum rituals

label: Elevator Karaoke
topic: Korean high‑rise elevators equipped with karaoke screens let riders sing on the way up
hook: Ever taken a ride up a skyscraper and found yourself belting out a pop song?
body: In several Seoul apartment complexes and office towers, elevators have built‑in touch screens, microphones and Bluetooth speakers. When the doors close, a short prompt invites passengers to choose a song and sing while the cabin moves. The feature is meant to turn a mundane commute into a social ice‑breaker, and many residents share videos of spontaneous duets on social media.
twist: Some elevators even display the current floor as scrolling lyrics, so the ride becomes a moving karaoke stage.
caveat: These karaoke elevators are found in a number of newer buildings, but they are not present in most older or low‑rise structures.
verify_note: Seoul elevator karaoke installation news, Korean architecture magazines, YouTube videos of elevator karaoke

label: T‑money Transfer Perk
topic: Seoul’s T‑money card gives a free subway fare when you transfer within 30 minutes
hook: Did you know you can ride two subway lines for the price of one in Seoul?
body: The T‑money transportation card, used for subways, buses and taxis, automatically applies a transfer discount if a passenger exits one line and boards another within 30 minutes at the same station. The system records the time stamp and deducts only the base fare for the second ride, effectively letting commuters explore the city with half the usual cost. Many tourists rely on this feature to hop between popular sites quickly.
twist: During special holidays like Chuseok, the transfer window is extended to 45 minutes in some lines.
caveat: The transfer discount applies only to subway lines operated by Seoul Metro and not to all private railways or express trains.
verify_note: Seoul Metro T‑money transfer policy, official Seoul transportation website, travel guide articles

label: Charging Bike‑Share
topic: Seoul’s public bikes sometimes let you charge your phone while you ride.
hook: Did you know you can plug your smartphone into a Seoul bike‑share and charge it on the go?
body: Seoul’s Ddareungi bike‑share system introduced a pilot in 2021 that equipped a handful of bicycles with built‑in USB ports. Riders can connect their phone to keep navigation apps and messages alive during the commute. The power comes from a small battery housed in the bike frame, recharged overnight at the docking station. The idea was launched to help commuters who rely heavily on mobile maps and contact apps.
twist: A few of those bikes even have a tiny solar panel on the handlebar that helps replenish the battery while you pedal.
caveat: This charging feature is available only at select bike‑share stations in Seoul and a few other major cities, not across the entire national system.
verify_note: Seoul bike share USB charging port 2021 Ddareungi charging bike pilot

label: Lobby Karaoke Booths
topic: Apartment complexes let residents book a tiny karaoke room in the building lobby for a quick song break
hook: Did you know many Seoul apartments have a karaoke booth right in the lobby you can reserve in seconds?
body: In several newer high‑rise apartment complexes in Seoul, a small sound‑proof karaoke room—often called a "lobby noraebang"—is installed on the first floor. Residents can book it through an app or a touchscreen panel for as little as 15 minutes, letting families or coworkers sing a song after dinner or before work. The rooms come with a song‑selection screen, a microphone, and even a small mirror, turning a brief break into a social ritual. This convenience reflects Korea’s love of karaoke and the trend of maximizing shared amenities in dense housing.
twist: Some buildings let you record your performance and automatically post it to a private building community board where neighbors can like and comment.
caveat: These lobby karaoke rooms are most common in newer complexes in Seoul and a few other large cities; older apartments and most suburban housing do not have them.
verify_note: Korean apartment shared karaoke room, lobby noraebang, apartment complex amenities Seoul

label: App‑Rented River BBQ
topic: Reserve a portable grill and picnic spot on the Han River through a smartphone app for a night‑time barbecue.
hook: Did you know you can book a grill on Seoul's Han River with just a tap?
body: In many Hangang parks, visitors can open the official 'Hangang Park' app, choose a free‑standing table or a grass spot, and add a portable gas grill to the reservation. The park staff delivers a small propane canister and a fold‑up grill to the chosen spot, letting friends or couples fire up samgyeopsal or chicken as the city lights reflect on the water. After the meal, a cleaning crew collects the grill, canister and any trash, so the area stays tidy without the diners having to lug everything home. The service blends Korea's love of outdoor eating with high‑tech convenience, turning a simple park visit into a coordinated mini‑event.
twist: Some parks even let you pre‑order a ready‑made BBQ kit with meat, sauces and side dishes, delivered right to your reserved grill.
caveat: The reservation system is available only at selected Hangang parks and requires the official app; not all riverside areas or private parks offer this service.
verify_note: Hangang Park app grill reservation, Seoul river BBQ rental, Han River portable grill service

label: Rooftop Community Gardens
topic: Residents grow vegetables on high‑rise apartment rooftops
hook: Did you know many Seoul apartments have their own rooftop farms where neighbors harvest together?
body: In several high‑rise complexes, especially in districts like Gangnam and Mapo, the management allocates small plots on the roof for residents to plant herbs, lettuce, and cherry tomatoes. Plots are usually rented for a modest monthly fee, and the harvested produce is often shared at communal meals or sold at a building‑wide market day. The initiative started as a way to add green space and reduce food mileage in dense urban areas. The gardens are tended by residents of all ages, turning the skyline into a patchwork of mini farms.
twist: Some rooftops even install hydroponic towers that can grow lettuce year‑round without soil.
caveat: These gardens are present in many newer apartment complexes, but not in older buildings or low‑rise neighborhoods.
verify_note: Seoul rooftop farms apartment community garden hydroponic tower

label: Dog‑Friendly Café Menus
topic: Cafés that serve treats specially made for dogs
hook: Ever seen a coffee shop where the dog gets a menu of its own?
body: In neighborhoods such as Hongdae and Itaewon, numerous cafés welcome patrons' pets and offer a separate ‘dog menu’ featuring rice‑based biscuits, meat‑flavored pupcakes, and even a tiny bowl of broth. Owners can order a latte while their dog enjoys a treat served on a small plate, and many places provide water bowls and dog‑friendly seating areas. The trend grew from the strong pet‑ownership culture and the desire for owners to socialize with their dogs in public spaces. Staff often photograph the canine customers for social‑media posts, adding to the café’s buzz.
twist: A few cafés even host weekly ‘puppy playdates’ where dogs can mingle while owners sip coffee.
caveat: Dog‑friendly cafés are common in trendy districts, but many traditional cafés and many public spaces still prohibit pets.
verify_note: Dog friendly cafés Seoul Hongdae dog menu pupcake

label: Instant Noodle Vending Machines
topic: Hot ramen dispensed from vending machines in stations and malls
hook: Imagine buying a steaming bowl of ramen from a vending machine without a kitchen.
body: Across Seoul’s subway stations, office buildings, and large malls, you’ll find vending machines that dispense hot instant noodles in a cup, complete with a built‑in heating element that boils water in about three minutes. Users simply insert cash or tap a contactless card, choose the flavor, and watch the machine prepare the meal behind a transparent window. The machines are maintained by companies that restock fresh packets daily, ensuring the noodles are hot and the broth flavorful. They are especially popular among late‑night commuters and students who need a quick, warm bite.
twist: Some machines even offer a side of kimchi or a soft‑boiled egg for an extra fee.
caveat: These machines are common in high‑traffic urban areas, but you’ll rarely see them in small towns or residential neighborhoods.
verify_note: Korean instant noodle vending machine Seoul subway hot ramen

label: Floating River Library
topic: A free book‑laden boat cruises the Han River offering reading spots for passersby
hook: Did you know Seoul has a floating library you can board for free?
body: During the warmer months, the Seoul Metropolitan Government operates a boat shaped like a bookshelf that travels along the Han River. Inside, wooden benches and shelves hold dozens of Korean and English titles, and visitors can sit, read, or borrow books on the spot. The boat stops at several riverside parks, letting commuters and families hop on during a stroll or bike ride. The service aims to promote reading culture and make literature accessible without a membership fee.
twist: The library even offers a small ‘story time’ corner where a volunteer reads aloud to children while the river flows by.
caveat: The floating library operates mainly on weekends and weekdays between April and October, and its route is limited to the central stretch of the Han River.
verify_note: Seoul floating library Han River, Seoul Metropolitan Government book boat, Hangang floating library schedule

label: Seafood Vending Machines
topic: Vending machines on Busan streets dispense fresh, ice‑cold fish and shellfish
hook: Can you buy live fish from a vending machine in Korea?
body: In Busan’s coastal neighborhoods, glass‑front vending machines stocked with chilled trays of mackerel, squid, and even live clams allow shoppers to select seafood with a button press. The machines are restocked early each morning by local fish markets, keeping the catch at near‑freshness, and they accept credit cards or mobile payments. After purchasing, customers often walk a short distance to nearby restaurants that cook the fish on the spot, turning a quick snack into a full meal. This convenience reflects South Korea’s blend of high tech and seafood culture.
twist: Some machines even feature a small digital screen showing the fish’s catch location and the time it was harvested, letting buyers track its freshness.
caveat: These machines are most common in Busan and a few other port cities; they are less prevalent inland and not all operate year‑round.
verify_note: Busan seafood vending machine, Korean vending machine fresh fish, live fish vending machine South Korea

label: Did You Eat? Greeting
topic: Koreans often ask “Did you eat?” as a casual hello, not a literal question about food.
hook: Ever been asked “Did you eat?” right after saying hello?
body: In many everyday situations—from a subway ride to a coffee shop—Koreans greet each other with 밥 먹었어요? (Did you eat?). It’s a way of checking on someone’s wellbeing, similar to “How are you?” The phrase can appear even when the person knows the other just finished a meal, turning a simple hello into a warm check‑in.
twist: The same question can also be a subtle invitation to share a quick snack if you’re near a street‑food stall.
caveat: This greeting is most common among friends, family, and older generations; younger people in formal settings may use different expressions.
verify_note: Korean greeting 밥 먹었어요? cultural etiquette
narration: Ever been asked “Did you eat?” right after saying hello? In Korea, that simple question—bap meogeosseoyo?—is a common greeting. You’ll hear it on the subway, in a coffee shop, or at a street‑food stall. It’s less about the meal and more about checking on someone’s wellbeing, much like “How are you?” Even if the person just finished a bite, the phrase turns a quick hello into a warm check‑in. Sometimes it doubles as a subtle invitation to share a snack nearby. The habit is most common among friends, family, and older generations, while younger folks in formal settings may choose other expressions. So the next time someone asks, you might just be getting a friendly hello—plus a possible snack offer.

label: Reusable Cup Lockers
topic: Some Seoul cafés let customers store personal reusable cups in keyless lockers for quick pick‑up.
hook: Imagine borrowing a coffee cup, locking it, and never losing it again.
body: Eco‑focused cafés in neighborhoods like Hongdae and Seongsu have installed small locker banks next to the counter. After you bring your own cup, you scan a QR code, the locker opens, and you store the cup; the system logs the locker number on your phone. When you return, you retrieve it without any exchange of keys, encouraging a zero‑waste habit while keeping your cup safe from being misplaced.
twist: A few of these lockers even charge a tiny fee that donates to local environmental NGOs.
caveat: Lockers are offered mainly by boutique or sustainability‑focused cafés, not by the majority of coffee shops across the city.
verify_note: Seoul café reusable cup lockers zero waste
narration: Imagine borrowing a coffee cup, locking it, and never losing it again. In Seoul, some eco‑focused cafés in neighborhoods like Hongdae and Seongsu have small locker banks right by the counter. You bring your own reusable cup, scan a QR code, and a locker pops open. The system logs the locker number on your phone, so you can drop the cup in and walk away. When you return, the same code opens the locker and you retrieve your cup—no keys needed. A few cafés even add a tiny fee that goes to local environmental NGOs. These lockers are offered mainly by boutique or sustainability‑focused cafés, not by most coffee shops in the city.

label: Morning Milk Bike Delivery
topic: Fresh milk is still delivered by bike to many apartment complexes before 8 am.
hook: Did you know you can get farm‑fresh milk delivered to your doorstep before school starts?
body: In residential districts such as Gangbuk and parts of Busan, local dairy vendors ride electric bikes through the early‑morning streets, stopping at apartment entrances to hand out chilled milk cartons. Residents often greet the rider by name, and the delivery schedule is posted on a community board, making it a ritual that has persisted despite supermarkets. The service is valued for its freshness and the personal connection it creates between the rider and the community.
twist: Some riders also hand out a small free sample of seasonal fruit jam as a thank‑you for regular customers.
caveat: Bike milk delivery is common in many but not all apartment complexes, especially those with active resident committees; larger high‑rise towers usually rely on grocery deliveries.
verify_note: Korean milk delivery by bike residential neighborhoods
narration: Did you know you can get farm‑fresh milk delivered to your doorstep before school starts? In neighborhoods like Gangbuk and parts of Busan, local dairy vendors hop on electric bikes just after sunrise. They zip through the quiet streets, stop at each apartment entrance, and hand out chilled milk cartons. Residents often greet the rider by name, and the delivery times are posted on a community board, turning it into a small daily ritual. Many riders even add a tiny free sample of seasonal fruit jam as a thank‑you for regular customers. The service isn’t everywhere—larger high‑rise towers usually rely on grocery deliveries—but it keeps a personal, fresh connection alive.
ko_title: 한국: 자전거 우유 배달, 학교 가기 전 아침에 우유
ko_description:
🎯 학교 가기 전, 농장에서 바로 짜낸 신선한 우유를 집 앞까지 배달받을 수 있다는 사실, 알고 계셨나요?

강북 및 부산 일부 지역 등 주거지에서 현지 유제품 판매업자들이 전동 자전거를 타고 이른 아침 거리를 누비며 아파트 입구에 들러 차가운 우유팩을 건네줍니다. 주민들은 종종 배달원의 이름을 부르며 인사하고, 배달 일정은 커뮤니티 게시판에 게시돼 슈퍼마켓이 있음에도 불구하고 지속되는 일종의 의식이 됩니다. 이 서비스는 신선함과 배달원과 지역 사회 사이에 형성되는 개인적인 연결 고리 때문에 가치를 인정받고 있습니다.

💡 일부 배달원은 정기 고객에게 감사의 의미로 계절 과일 잼 소량을 무료 샘플로 제공하기도 합니다.

label: Smart Elevator Queue
topic: New high‑rise apartments use smartphone apps to assign virtual elevator tickets, cutting wait times.
hook: What if you could reserve an elevator slot from your phone before you even reach the lobby?
body: Buildings like the Lotte World Tower and newer complexes in Songpa have installed “smart elevator” systems. Residents tap a button on a dedicated app, select their floor, and receive a digital ticket that shows up on the lobby screen. The elevators group passengers heading to similar floors, so the lobby line shortens dramatically. The system also alerts you when the elevator is arriving, letting you time your coffee break perfectly.
twist: During peak hours, the app can reroute you to a nearby stairwell that has a moving walkway, offering a faster alternative.
caveat: These systems are limited to recently built high‑rise apartments and office towers; older buildings still rely on traditional button calls.

label: Underground Parcel Lockers
topic: How Koreans receive online orders without meeting couriers
hook: Ever wonder how a Korean apartment gets a package without anyone at the door?
body: In many newer apartment complexes, couriers drop parcels into a secure underground locker that has dozens of individual compartments. The resident’s phone receives a push notification with a QR code, which they scan at the locker’s panel to open the specific box. This system lets the delivery happen 24 hours a day, even when the building is closed, and it reduces missed deliveries. Residents often watch the locker doors open on a small screen as they retrieve their items.
twist: Some of these lockers are climate‑controlled, keeping groceries like fresh milk or salads at the right temperature until the owner picks them up.
caveat: The locker system is most common in high‑rise apartments in Seoul and a few other major cities; older buildings and rural areas still rely on door‑to‑door delivery.

ko_title: 한국: 지하 사물함 QR로 사물함 열기
ko_description:
🎯 한국 아파트에서 누가 문 앞에 있지 않아도 택배를 받는 방법이 궁금하신가요?

많은 최신 아파트 단지에서는 택배 기사가 수십 개의 개별 구획이 있는 안전한 지하 사물함에 택배를 넣습니다. 거주자의 휴대폰에 QR 코드가 포함된 푸시 알림이 오고, 이를 사물함 패널에 스캔하면 해당 칸이 열립니다. 이 시스템 덕분에 건물이 닫혀 있어도 24시간 내내 배송이 가능하고, 미배달이 줄어듭니다. 주민들은 물건을 꺼낼 때 작은 화면에 사물함 문이 열리는 모습을 볼 수 있습니다.

💡 일부 사물함은 온도 조절이 되어 있어, 신선한 우유나 샐러드 같은 식품을 주인이 찾을 때까지 적정 온도로 보관합니다.

label: School Banchan Buffet
topic: Students serve themselves side dishes in Korean school cafeterias
hook: Did you know Korean kids pick their own side dishes at lunch, just like a buffet?
body: In many public elementary and middle schools, the cafeteria presents a rotating tray of banchan—small side dishes such as kimchi, seasoned spinach, and rolled omelet. Students line up, take a plate, and choose the banchan they like, while the teacher often joins the line to eat with them. The dishes are portion‑controlled, and the staff refills the tray every few minutes, keeping the food fresh. Some schools let students vote via a tablet for the next week’s banchan menu, giving them a voice in the menu planning.
twist: A few districts have introduced a 'zero‑waste' rule where students can only take as many side dishes as they finish, dramatically cutting food waste.
caveat: This self‑serve style is typical in public schools in larger cities; private schools may use pre‑served meals.

많은 초·중학교 식당에서는 김치, 시금치나물, 계란말이 같은 작은 반찬이 담긴 회전식 그릇을 제공합니다. 학생들은 줄을 서서 접시를 집고 원하는 반찬을 고릅니다. 분량은 조절되며 직원이 몇 분마다 그릇을 다시 채워줍니다. 일부 학교는 학생들이 다음 주 반찬 메뉴를 태블릿으로 제안하도록 허용해 목소리를 내게 합니다. 일부 교육구는 학생들이 마무리할 수 있는 양만 가져가도록 권장해 낭비를 줄이려 합니다.

💡 이 자가서비스 방식은 도시 학교에서 흔하지만, 사립학교는 미리 담아 놓은 식사를 제공할 수 있습니다.

label: NFC Café Study Pods
topic: Tables that silence phones automatically for focused study
hook: Imagine a café table that makes your phone go silent the moment you sit down.
body: Several chain cafés in Seoul embed NFC tags in the tops of their private study pods. When a patron taps their phone, an app switches the device to silent mode, disables notifications, and even starts a Pomodoro timer. The pod also offers adjustable LED lighting and a built‑in air purifier that syncs with the timer, creating a personalized focus environment. After the session, a second tap restores the phone’s normal settings.
twist: Some locations reward completed focus sessions with a small free drink voucher that appears in the app.
caveat: These NFC‑enabled pods are currently limited to major café chains in central Seoul and a handful of other cities; most independent cafés still rely on manual signs.

label: Hanbok Tea Welcome
topic: Tourists try on hanbok and receive a traditional tea greeting
hook: Step into a hanbok and be served a cup of tea—South Korea’s sweet welcome for visitors.
body: At cultural villages and heritage sites such as Bukchon Hanok Village, visitors can rent a hanbok for a short period and walk the historic streets in traditional dress. After dressing, staff in the hanok tea house offer a small cup of warm jujube‑infused tea, explaining its calming properties and its role in Korean hospitality. The gesture is meant to make tourists feel part of the culture and often includes a brief lesson on proper tea‑drinking etiquette. Many tourists share the experience on social media, sparking a modern revival of hanbok wear.
twist: The tea is sometimes served in a miniature ceramic bowl that matches the hanbok’s color palette, creating a coordinated visual experience.
caveat: The service is most common in designated heritage zones and larger tourist attractions; smaller museums may not provide the tea.

label: Office Nap Pods
topic: Quiet rooms in Korean offices where employees can take short power naps
hook: Did you know many Korean offices have secret nap rooms you can slip into after lunch?
body: In a growing number of South Korean companies, a small room equipped with a reclining chair, dim lighting and a timer is set aside for employees to rest for 10–20 minutes. The idea gained traction after studies showed that brief naps can improve afternoon alertness, and firms such as Samsung and Naver have installed them in their headquarters. Workers usually book the slot via an internal app or simply knock and wait for a free spot. The practice is still optional and more common in tech‑oriented firms than in traditional manufacturing sites.
twist: Some companies even provide a gentle alarm that plays a short K‑pop melody to wake nap‑takers.
caveat: Nap rooms are present mainly in larger corporations and startups in Seoul; smaller firms and many public‑sector offices often do not have them.

label: Power‑Bank Rental Kiosks
topic: QR‑based portable charger rentals found at subway stations and malls
hook: Your phone dies on the subway? You can rent a power bank from a kiosk in minutes.
body: Across Seoul, vending‑style kiosks let you borrow a portable charger by scanning a QR code with your smartphone; you pay a small fee and keep the device for a few hours before returning it to any other kiosk. The service, launched by companies such as KT and LG U+, is aimed at commuters and tourists who don’t want to carry their own charger. The kiosks are usually located near station exits, and the return process is automated, requiring only another QR scan. While the system is widespread in the capital, similar stations are fewer in provincial cities.
twist: Some kiosks also display real‑time weather forecasts and subway arrival times on the same screen.
caveat: The rental service is most common in Seoul’s major lines and large malls; not all subway stations or smaller towns have these kiosks.
verify_note: Seoul power bank rental kiosk, KT power bank rental, LG U+ portable charger rental

label: Rooftop Picnic Gardens
topic: Residents use apartment rooftops for casual picnics and socialising
hook: Ever seen a city skyline turned into a weekend picnic spot?
body: Many high‑rise apartment complexes in Seoul reserve a portion of their roof as a communal garden, complete with benches, grills, and a small herb plot. On Saturdays, groups of friends bring simple snacks, a Bluetooth speaker, and enjoy a view of the city while chatting, effectively creating a park in the sky. Because the space is shared among all residents, it’s common for neighbours you’ve never met to join in a spontaneous gathering. The trend grew as urban dwellers sought outdoor space without leaving the building.
twist: Some rooftops even host pop‑up yoga classes early in the morning, led by resident instructors.
caveat: Access is limited to residents of the specific apartment complex; the amenity is more typical in newer developments and less common in older low‑rise neighborhoods.
verify_note: Seoul apartment rooftop garden picnic, communal rooftop space Korea, rooftop garden Seoul

label: Subway Wi‑Fi & Seat Screens
topic: Free high‑speed internet and seat‑back displays on Seoul subway trains
hook: You can stream a drama while riding the subway thanks to free Wi‑Fi and seat screens.
body: Since 2020, every line of the Seoul Metropolitan Subway provides complimentary high‑speed Wi‑Fi, and many newer train sets feature seat‑back LCD panels that show news, weather and short ads. Commuters often use the connection to watch Korean dramas, catch up on work emails, or play mobile games during the 30‑ to 60‑minute ride. The service is managed by the Seoul Metropolitan Rapid Transit Corporation and is funded through advertising displayed on the screens. While Wi‑Fi is generally reliable in central lines, some outer‑city routes may experience occasional outages.
twist: During peak hours, the system automatically prioritises streaming video for a smoother viewing experience.
caveat: Free Wi‑Fi and seat‑back screens are available on most lines in Seoul, but not on all regional or intercity trains outside the capital.
verify_note: Seoul subway free WiFi, subway seat back screens, SMRT WiFi service

label: Phone Pouch Silence
topic: Study cafés give phones a transparent bag to keep them silent
hook: Ever seen a phone disappear into a clear bag before studying?
body: Many Korean study cafés and university libraries provide small transparent pouches where patrons place their smartphones at the start of a session. The pouch stays on the table, visually reminding everyone the device is muted, which helps maintain a quiet environment. The practice grew from the high density of students who use phones for both study and distraction, turning a simple bag into a social cue for silence.
twist: Some cafés even lock the pouch with a tiny padlock that only opens when you leave, preventing you from taking the phone back mid‑session.
caveat: The practice is common in many urban study cafés and university libraries, but it is not universal across all Korean eateries or homes.

ko_title: 한국: 카페 전화 무음 가방에 전화 숨기기
ko_description:
🎯 공부하기 전에 투명 가방에 전화가 사라지는 걸 본 적 있나요?

많은 한국의 스터디 카페와 대학 도서관에서는 손님들이 세션 시작 시 스마트폰을 넣는 작은 투명 파우치를 제공합니다. 파우치는 테이블 위에 남아 있어 기기가 무음 상태임을 시각적으로 상기시켜 주어 조용한 환경을 유지하는 데 도움이 됩니다. 이 관행은 공부와 동시에 휴대폰을 사용하는 학생들의 밀집도가 높아지면서, 단순한 가방이 침묵을 위한 사회적 신호로 변한 결과입니다.

💡 일부 카페는 파우치를 작은 자물쇠로 잠그기도 하는데, 이는 떠날 때만 열 수 있어 세션 중에 전화기를 다시 가져가는 것을 방지합니다.

label: Bike‑Rental Helmet Kiosk
topic: Bike‑share stations in Seoul also dispense helmets from a small vending machine.
hook: Did you know you can rent a bike and get a helmet from a vending machine in Seoul?
body: In many districts of Seoul, public bike‑share stations are paired with compact kiosks that store helmets. When you scan the bike’s QR code, the kiosk releases a clean helmet that fits the bike’s lock. The helmet is returned to the same kiosk when you finish your ride, and the system tracks usage automatically. This setup encourages safe cycling without the need to carry your own helmet.
twist: Some kiosks even sanitize the helmet with UV light between uses.
caveat: Helmet vending is available at many, but not all, bike‑share stations, primarily in central Seoul and certain pilot neighborhoods.

ko_title: 한국: 서울 자전거 공유 헬멧 키오스크에서
ko_description:
🎯 서울에서 자전거를 대여하고 헬멧을 자동 판매기에서 받을 수 있다는 사실, 알고 계셨나요?

서울의 많은 구역에서는 공공 자전거 공유 스테이션과 헬멧을 보관하는 소형 키오스크가 함께 배치되어 있습니다. 자전거 QR 코드를 스캔하면, 키오스크가 자전거 잠금 장치에 맞는 깨끗한 헬멧을 내놓습니다. 라이딩을 마치면 같은 키오스크에 헬멧을 반납하고, 시스템이 자동으로 이용 현황을 추적합니다. 이 시스템은 개인 헬멧을 휴대할 필요 없이 안전한 자전거 이용을 장려합니다.

💡 일부 키오스크는 사용 사이에 UV 빛으로 헬멧을 살균하기도 합니다.

label: Women‑Only Subway Cars
topic: Designated women‑only subway cars operate during rush hour on several Seoul lines.
hook: Ever seen a subway car reserved just for women in Seoul?
body: During the morning and evening peak hours, Seoul Metro marks one car on lines such as Line 2 and Line 4 as women‑only. The doors open with a pink sign and a brief announcement, and the car is kept separate from the mixed‑gender cars. Many commuters appreciate the extra sense of security, especially during crowded trips. The policy has been in place since 2012 and is enforced by station staff.
twist: During special holidays, the women‑only car sometimes carries a small free gift, like a hand‑sanitizer packet.
caveat: The women‑only cars operate only on select lines during specific peak periods; not all trains or stations have them.

ko_title: 한국: 여성 전용 지하철 러시아워 핑크 차량?
ko_description:
🎯 서울에서 여성 전용 지하철 차량을 본 적 있나요?

출퇴근 러시아워에 서울 지하철은 2호선·4호선 등 일부 노선에서 한 칸을 여성 전용으로 지정합니다. 문이 열릴 때 핑크 색 표지판과 짧은 안내 방송이 나오며, 해당 차량은 남녀가 섞인 차량과 구분됩니다. 많은 승객이 특히 혼잡한 시간대에 보안감이 높아진다는 점을 만족합니다. 이 정책은 2012년부터 시행돼 역 직원이 단속합니다.

💡 특별 공휴일에는 여성 전용 차량에 손소독제 한 팩 등 작은 무료 선물을 제공하기도 합니다.

label: QR Code Street Food
topic: Scan, pay, and eat street food without cash
hook: Did you know you can order tteokbokki by scanning a QR code on the stall?
body: In busy districts such as Hongdae and Myeongdong, many street‑food stalls display a small QR‑code sign beside their grill. Customers open a Korean mobile‑payment app, scan the code, choose the dish, and pay instantly; the vendor then hands over the hot plate. The system grew after the pandemic as a way to reduce cash handling and speed up service, and it works with popular apps like KakaoPay and Naver Pay. As a result, queues often move faster than at nearby cash‑only stalls.
twist: Some vendors also let you add a tip for the chef through the same QR‑code interface.
caveat: This practice is common in urban street‑food areas that have partnered with payment platforms, but many traditional markets and rural stalls still rely on cash only.

label: Seoul Subway Quiet Car
topic: Designated silent cars for commuters who want to study or rest
hook: Ever seen a whole subway car whispering in Seoul?
body: On lines such as Line 9 and a few others, one carriage is marked as a “quiet car” with signs that ask passengers to keep phones on silent and refrain from loud conversations. During the morning and evening rush, some passengers may open laptops, carry notebooks, or read e‑books, creating a study‑like environment. The policy was introduced to give densely packed riders a space for focused work and to reduce overall cabin noise. Announcements remind riders that the quiet car is not for phone calls or music playback.
twist: During peak hours, the quiet car can become crowded, and some commuters may seek a seat for work or rest.
caveat: Quiet cars are available only on certain subway lines and primarily during weekday peak periods; not all trains or stations have them.

label: Heated Toilet Seats
topic: Public restrooms in many Korean cities have heated toilet seats that turn on automatically in winter.
hook: Did you know that some Korean public toilets have seats that can warm up before you sit?
body: In some Seoul department stores, subway stations, and hospitals, public restrooms have sensor‑activated heated seats that may start warming when someone approaches. The seats are powered electrically, often drawing electricity from the building’s supply, so they stay warm during the cold winter months. When you move away, the heating often shuts off after a short period of inactivity to save energy. This convenience reflects Korea’s focus on hygiene and user comfort in public spaces.
twist: Many of those modern seats also hide a bidet nozzle, letting you adjust water pressure with a single button for a quick clean.
caveat: Heated seats are common in newer urban public facilities, but older or rural restrooms may not have them.

ko_title: 시원한 좌석, 한국에서 앉기 전 따뜻해지는 좌석
ko_description:
🎯 한국의 일부 공중 화장실에 좌석이 앉기 전에 따뜻해지는 기능이 있다는 것을 알고 계셨나요?

서울의 일부 백화점, 지하철역, 병원에서는 감지 센서가 작동해 사람이 접근하면 좌석이 따뜻해지는 공중 화장실이 있습니다. 좌석은 전기적으로 구동되며, 대부분 건물의 전력 공급을 이용해 전기를 끌어와 겨울철에도 따뜻함을 유지합니다. 사용자가 멀어지면 에너지를 절약하기 위해 짧은 비활성 기간 후에 난방이 자동으로 꺼집니다. 이러한 편의성은 한국이 공공장소에서 위생과 사용자 편안함을 중시한다는 것을 반영합니다.

💡 그 현대적인 좌석 중 상당수는 비데 노즐을 숨겨 두고 있어 버튼 하나로 물압을 조절해 빠르게 세척할 수 있습니다.

label: Zero‑Waste Bulk Aisles
topic: Supermarkets and some convenience stores set aside bulk sections where shoppers bring their own containers to fill grains, nuts, and spices.
hook: In Korea, you can shop the bulk aisle without buying a single plastic bag.
body: Major Korean grocery chains such as Emart, Homeplus, and Lotte Mart have introduced “zero‑waste” aisles where customers bring reusable jars or bags to fill items like rice, beans, tea, and nuts. Staff weigh the containers before and after filling to charge the correct amount, and the practice grew out of a government‑backed campaign to cut plastic waste that began in the 2010s. Younger shoppers in city neighborhoods often favor these sections for both environmental and cost reasons. The system works much like bulk shopping in Europe, but with a Korean focus on precise weighing and labeling.
twist: Some stores even offer a small discount for using your own container, encouraging repeat visits.
caveat: Zero‑waste bulk sections are available in many large supermarkets and some convenience stores in major cities, but not in smaller neighborhood shops.

ko_title: 한국 제로 웨이스트 플라스틱백이 필요없어요
ko_description:
🎯 한국에서는 플라스틱백 한 개도 사지 않고 벌크 코너에서 쇼핑할 수 있어요.

에마트, 홈플러스, 롯데마트 같은 대형 한국 식료품 체인점에서는 고객이 재사용 가능한 병이나 가방을 가져와 쌀, 콩, 차, 견과류 등을 채우는 "제로‑웨이스트" 코너를 도입했습니다. 직원은 채우기 전후에 용기를 무게를 재어 정확한 금액을 청구하고, 이 관행은 2010년대에 시작된 정부 후원 캠페인에서 플라스틱 쓰레기를 줄이기 위해 발전했습니다. 도시 지역의 젊은 쇼핑객들은 환경과 비용 두 가지 이유로 이 섹션을 선호합니다. 이 시스템은 유럽의 벌크 쇼핑과 비슷하지만 한국식으로 정밀한 무게 측정과 라벨링이 강조됩니다.

💡 일부 매장에서는 자체 용기를 사용하면 소정의 할인도 제공해 재방문을 유도합니다.

label: Automated Bike Parking
topic: Multi‑story bike‑parking towers in Seoul automatically lift and store bicycles, freeing ground space.
hook: Ever seen a skyscraper for bikes that lifts your ride up like an elevator?
body: In districts such as Gangnam, Songpa, and near several subway stations, public bike‑parking towers use a conveyor‑belt system that lifts a bike into a stacked compartment after the rider scans a QR code. The towers can store dozens of bicycles in the footprint of a single parking spot, and users retrieve their bike by scanning the same code, which lowers the platform back to ground level. This solution helps the city promote cycling while managing limited sidewalk space. Many of the towers also include charging ports for electric‑bike users.
twist: The towers are equipped with charging ports, so electric bike users can top up while their bike is stored.
caveat: These automated towers are installed at selected subway stations and public parks, not at every bike‑share dock across the city.

ko_title: 한국: 서울 자전거 타워, 코드로 승강되는 자전거 리프트

🎯 엘리베이터처럼 자전거를 올려주는 초고층 자전거 타워를 본 적이 있나요?

강남, 송파 등 여러 구역과 지하철역 근처에 공공 자전거 주차 타워가 있습니다. 이 타워는 컨베이어 벨트 시스템을 이용해 QR 코드를 스캔하면 자전거를 쌓인 칸으로 올려 놓습니다. 한 개의 주차 공간 안에 수십 대의 자전거를 보관할 수 있고, 같은 코드를 다시 스캔하면 플랫폼이 내려와 자전거를 꺼낼 수 있습니다. 이 솔루션은 시내에서 자전거 이용을 장려하면서 보행자 도로 공간을 효율적으로 관리하도록 돕습니다. 많은 타워에는 전기 자전거 사용자용 충전 포트도 포함돼 있습니다.

label: App‑Controlled Floor Heating
topic: Many new Korean apartments let residents pre‑heat the ondol floor with a smartphone app
hook: Ever turned on your floor heating while still on the subway?
body: In several high‑rise apartments built after 2015, the under‑floor heating (ondol) is linked to a building‑wide IoT system. Residents can open an app, set the temperature, and schedule the heating to start before they arrive home. The system often shows real‑time energy use, encouraging people to warm the rooms only when needed. This convenience grew from the dense commuter lifestyle, where coming home to a cold floor is common.
twist: Some complexes even let you sync the heating schedule with the city’s public‑transport arrival data, so the floor warms automatically when your train is a few minutes away.
caveat: The feature is mainly available in newer apartments in major cities like Seoul and Busan; older buildings and many suburban units still use manual thermostats.

ko_title: 한국: 지하철에서 온돌 가열, 따뜻한 타일에 도착
ko_description:
🎯 아직도 지하철에 타고 있을 때 바닥 난방을 켜본 적 있나요?

서울과 부산의 최신 고층 아파트 중 일부는 온돌 시스템을 건물 전체 IoT 네트워크와 연동할 수 있습니다. 스마트폰 앱을 열어 목표 온도를 설정하고, 집에 도착하기 전에 난방이 시작되도록 예약할 수 있습니다. 앱에서는 예상 에너지 사용량을 표시하고 어느 방을 난방할지 선택할 수 있게 합니다. 이러한 편리함은 장거리 통근 후 집으로 돌아오는 사람들이 많은 한국의 밀집 통근 생활 방식과 맞아떨어집니다. 몇몇 단지는 대중교통 도착 시간과 난방 스케줄을 맞추는 실험을 진행 중이며, 열차가 도착하기 직전에 바닥을 켜는 방식입니다. 이 기능은 주로 대도시의 최신 아파트에서 더 많이 나타나고, 오래된 건물이나 교외 주택은 여전히 수동 온도 조절기에 의존하고 있습니다.

label: KakaoTalk Gifticon Culture
topic: South Koreans frequently send digital coupons called ‘gifticons’ via KakaoTalk, redeemable instantly at stores
hook: Can you buy a coffee for a friend without ever leaving your chat?
body: KakaoTalk, the dominant messaging app, introduced ‘gifticons’—scannable digital coupons for coffee, meals, or cosmetics—that users can purchase and send directly in a chat. The recipient receives a QR code that can be shown on their phone and redeemed at the merchant’s counter within seconds. Because the process is integrated with payment and loyalty systems, many cafés and retailers report a surge in impulse purchases triggered by a friend’s message. The practice has become a common way to celebrate birthdays, thank coworkers, or simply treat a friend on the spot.
twist: During major sales events, some brands release limited‑edition gifticons that are only available for a few hours, turning the chat into a fast‑paced flash sale arena.
caveat: Gifticon usage is most prevalent among KakaoTalk users in urban areas and among younger demographics; older generations or those who prefer other messengers may use traditional paper coupons.

ko_title: 한국: 카카오톡 기프티콘 커피를 채팅으로?
ko_description:
🎯 채팅을 떠나지 않고도 친구에게 커피를 사줄 수 있나요?

카카오톡, 국내 메신저 시장을 장악한 앱은 ‘기프티콘’—커피, 식사, 화장품 등 디지털 쿠폰을 스캔해 사용할 수 있는—을 도입했습니다. 사용자는 채팅 안에서 바로 구매해 보낼 수 있습니다. 받는 사람은 휴대폰에 QR 코드를 받아 매장 카운터에서 몇 초 만에 제시하고 교환합니다. 결제와 포인트 적립 시스템이 연동돼 있어 많은 카페와 소매점이 친구의 메시지에 의해 즉흥 구매가 급증했다고 보고합니다. 이 방식은 생일 축하, 직장 동료에게 감사 표시, 혹은 순간적인 선물 등으로 일반화되었습니다.

💡 대형 세일 기간에는 일부 브랜드가 몇 시간만 제공되는 한정판 기프티콘을 출시해 채팅을 빠른 플래시 세일 현장으로 만들기도 합니다.

label: Toilet Sound Mask
topic: Public restrooms often have bidet toilets that play a short tune to hide bathroom noises
hook: Did you know many Korean toilets can play a song to cover up bathroom sounds?
body: When a traveler steps into a Seoul subway station restroom, they may notice a small button on the bidet control panel. Pressing it triggers a brief melody that plays while the toilet flushes, helping to mask any sounds and protect privacy. This feature is built into many modern public toilets across the city, reflecting Korea's emphasis on personal comfort and discretion in shared spaces. The sound usually stops automatically after a few seconds, letting users focus on their business without embarrassment.
twist: Some models even let users choose between different sounds, such as a classical tune or a nature chirp, by tapping a selector on the panel.
caveat: The sound‑masking function is common in newer public restrooms in major cities and newer buildings, but many older facilities or rural locations still lack it.

topic: Korean schools recycle leftover meals into animal feed, shown on a daily scoreboard

label: QR Code Parking
topic: Scan‑and‑pay curbside parking replaces meters in many Seoul districts.
hook: In Seoul, you can park your car without a meter—just a QR code!
body: Since 2021, many streets in Seoul have installed QR‑code stickers on parking spaces. Drivers pull up, scan the code with a payment app, select the desired time, and pay instantly. The system sends a digital receipt to the driver’s phone and automatically lifts the restriction after the paid period. It removes the need for coin‑operated meters and speeds up the parking process.
twist: The QR code also displays real‑time availability of nearby EV charging spots when you scan it.
caveat: The QR‑code system is limited to certain districts like Jongno and Mapo; other neighborhoods still use traditional meters or free street parking.

label: Free Book Vending Machines
topic: Subway stations host book‑vending machines where you can borrow a paperback for free using your transit card.
hook: Did you know you can pick up a novel from a vending machine while waiting for the train?
body: In several Seoul Metro stations, compact vending machines dispense paperback books that commuters can take by tapping their T‑money card. The system records the transaction, and you’re expected to return the book within two weeks at any participating station. The selection rotates weekly, offering everything from best‑selling novels to travel guides, encouraging reading on the go. The machines are placed near exits, making a quick literary stop part of the daily commute.
twist: Some machines also accept a small donation, allowing you to support local libraries while borrowing.
caveat: The free‑book service operates only in select stations like Hongik‑univ and Gwanghwamun, and not all lines have these machines.

topic: Small robots collect disposable coffee cups in some Seoul cafés and reward users
hook: Did you know a tiny robot can turn your coffee cup into a free drink?

caveat: This setup is found mainly in trendy cafés in Seoul and a few other major cities, not in all coffee shops nationwide.

label: Midnight Convenience Store Dinner
topic: Workers often eat hot meals from 24‑hour convenience stores after night shifts
hook: Ever had a restaurant‑style dinner from a corner convenience store at 2 am?
body: In many Korean cities, 24‑hour convenience stores stay open through the night, offering hot items like ramen, tteokbokki, and even freshly fried chicken. Night‑shift employees often line up at the counter, where the staff heat the food on the spot and hand it over with a friendly bow, making the experience feel like a quick diner visit. Because the stores are everywhere, a quick dinner can be grabbed within a few minutes of finishing work. The practice has become a cultural norm for late‑working crowds.
twist: Some stores also provide free hot water and a small napkin, treating the customer like a regular restaurant patron.
caveat: This habit is common among night‑shift workers in urban areas; it may be less prevalent in rural regions where 24‑hour stores are rarer.

label: Cheering with ‘Fighting!’
topic: Koreans use the English‑sounding word “Fighting!” to cheer each other on
hook: What does ‘Fighting!’ really mean when Koreans shout it before an exam?
body: When a friend is about to take a test or start a competition, many Koreans will raise their fist and shout “Fighting!” (pronounced “pait‑ing”). The expression is borrowed from English but is used as an encouraging exclamation, similar to “You can do it!” in Korean. It’s heard in schools, workplaces, and even on TV shows, creating a shared moment of motivation. The gesture often includes a light fist‑pump, adding a visual cue to the verbal cheer.
twist: The word became so popular that it was added to the Korean language dictionary in the early 2000s as a loanword.
caveat: While widely understood, the usage varies; some older generations may prefer more traditional cheers, and it’s more common among younger speakers.

label: 5G Everywhere on the Subway
topic: Most Seoul subway trains now have nationwide 5G coverage, enabling seamless streaming
hook: Can you binge‑watch a drama on a moving subway without buffering?
body: In Seoul, the public transit authority partnered with telecom providers to install 5G antennas in subway tunnels and stations, giving many lines full‑speed coverage. As a result, commuters can stream high‑definition video, play online games, or join video calls while the train is in motion, often with no noticeable lag. The reliable connection has turned the subway into a mobile office and entertainment hub for many passengers. Tech‑savvy users often share screenshots of flawless streaming as proof.

label: Office Morning Greeting
topic: Many Korean workplaces start the day with a brief group bow and a shouted “Good morning!”
hook: Did you know Korean offices line up for a morning cheer before work begins?
body: In numerous companies, especially larger ones in Seoul, employees gather at the entrance, place their hands together in a slight bow, and say “Good morning” in unison. The ritual lasts only a few seconds but is meant to boost morale and show respect for colleagues. It often follows a quick clap or the chant “Fighting!” to energize the team. The practice is more common in traditional or public‑sector firms than in all start‑ups.
twist: Some firms even keep a leaderboard of the loudest morning cheers, awarding small prizes each month.
caveat: This ritual is not universal; many modern tech companies skip it and adopt a more informal start.
